config.title: Hitler's Bunker Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: Honest answers about the site of Hitler's bunker in Berlin: where it is, what you will actually find, whether you can go inside, why it is left unmarked, and how to visit it respectfully.

items.q: Where was Hitler's bunker in Berlin, and where is the site today?
items.a: The Führerbunker was an underground shelter beneath the garden of the old Reich Chancellery, near Wilhelmstraße in Mitte. It is where Hitler spent his final weeks and died on 30 April 1945. Today the exact spot is an ordinary residential car park at the corner of In den Ministergärten and Gertrud-Kolmar-Straße, right next to the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe and about a three to five minute walk from Potsdamer Platz.

items.q: Can you visit or go inside Hitler's bunker?
items.a: No. The bunker is sealed and buried, and there is no entrance and nothing to go into. The Soviets tried to demolish it in 1947, East Germany worked on it from 1959, and remaining sections were destroyed or sealed during construction of the current housing in 1988 to 1990. A few corridors are said to survive underground, but they are closed off and not accessible to the public. What you visit today is the surface: a car park and one information board.

One small bilingual information board (German and English), installed in 2006 by the Berliner Unterwelten association, with a simple diagram of the bunker layout. Around it is a residential car park and apartment blocks built by East Germany at the end of the 1980s. There is no statue, no museum and no marker on the ground itself, which is exactly why so many visitors walk straight past it.

items.q: Why is the site unmarked and just a car park?
items.a: The plainness is a deliberate choice. Germany decided not to make the spot easy to find or dramatic, so it would not become a shrine or a pilgrimage site for the far right. Even the 2006 board was kept understated, meant as a factual record rather than a memorial. The powerful memorial on this block is the neighbouring Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, which honours the victims rather than the man who caused their deaths.

items.q: How do I get to the Führerbunker site?
items.a: It sits between Ebertstraße and Wilhelmstraße in Mitte. From Potsdamer Platz, walk north up Ebertstraße along the edge of the Tiergarten, then turn east into Gertrud-Kolmar-Straße; the board is on the corner. From the Holocaust Memorial it is a two minute walk east. The nearest U-Bahn stops are Mohrenstraße (U2) and Brandenburger Tor (S1, S2, S25, U5).

items.q: What else should I see nearby to understand this history?
items.a: The area is dense with Nazi-era and Cold War history. Within a short walk you have the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, the Topography of Terror on the site of the former SS and Gestapo headquarters, and Bebelplatz, where the 1933 book burning took place. These places explain the period far more honestly than the empty car park can, and they are the better use of your time if you want to actually understand what happened.
